title: How Many Coats of Paint Do You Need? A Room-by-Room Guide
description: Two coats is the usual answer, but not always. When one coat is enough, when you need three, and how primer changes the count.
seoTitle: How Many Coats of Paint Do You Need?

cover.alt: Three stripes of navy paint on a white wall showing one, two and three coats

takeaways: Two coats is the standard for walls. Behr says most paint projects need two coats for full coverage.
One coat can work when you repaint the same or a similar color over sound, clean walls.
Dark colors, big color changes and bare surfaces often need a primer plus two coats, or three coats of paint.
body:
"Two coats" is the answer you will hear in any paint store, and most of the time it is right. Behr's own how-to guide says most paint projects need two coats for full coverage. But there are rooms where one coat does the job, and rooms where two is not enough. Knowing which one you are dealing with saves either a gallon of paint or a patchy wall that looks fine at noon and streaky at sunset.

## The quick guide

| Situation | Coats | Primer first? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same color, walls in good shape | 1, sometimes 2 | No |
| Similar color, a shade lighter or darker | 2 | No |
| Light color over a dark one | 2 or 3 | Yes, ideally tinted |
| Dark or bold color (deep red, navy, black) | 2, often 3 | Gray-tinted primer helps |
| New drywall | 2 | Yes, a drywall primer |
| Patched or stained walls | 2 | Spot-prime the patches and stains |
| Ceiling, white over white | 1 or 2 | No |
| Trim and doors | 2 | Only on bare wood or glossy old paint |
| Exterior siding | 2 | On bare wood and repairs |

## Why two coats is the default

Paint has two jobs: hide what is underneath and leave a film thick enough to wear well. One coat, rolled at the thickness the can recommends, rarely does both. You end up with "flashing", where some spots look shinier than others, and with roller marks that show in side light.

A second coat evens out the color and the sheen, fills in thin spots and gives the finish its intended thickness. It is also what scrubs and bumps wear through first, so walls in hallways and kids' rooms last longer with two.

## When one coat is enough

One coat can work if all of these are true:

- The new color is the same as the old one, or very close.
- The old paint is clean, sound and not glossy.
- You are using a good paint that hides well.
- You are not covering patches, stains or bare spots.

Some brands now sell paints that promise one-coat hide. Behr, for example, guarantees one-coat hide for its Dynasty and Marquee lines, but only in specific colors from its one-coat collection. The guarantee excludes uncoated, porous, heavily textured or repaired surfaces, which need more than one coat anyway. In other words, one-coat paint works best in exactly the situations where one coat of ordinary paint would have been close to enough.

A practical test: paint one coat on a whole wall, let it dry, then look at it with the light coming from the side. If you can see the old color, roller lines or dull patches, it needs a second.

## When you need three coats

- **Deep, saturated colors.** Reds, yellows and very dark blues are made with pigments that hide poorly. Behr notes that dark shades like black often need two full coats, and sometimes a third.
- **Light over dark.** Covering a navy accent wall with off-white can take three coats. A tinted primer usually brings it back to primer plus two.
- **Cheap paint.** Budget paint has less pigment, so you make up the difference with more coats and more labor.

## Where primer fits

Primer is not just "more paint". It seals porous surfaces, blocks stains and helps paint stick to glossy or slick surfaces. A coat of primer often replaces a coat of paint on a hard job, and it is usually cheaper per gallon.

Use primer on new drywall, bare wood, patches, water or smoke stains, and before a big color change. Our [primer calculator](/blog/primer-calculator/) tells you how much to buy and walks through each case.

## How long to wait between coats

Behr's guidance for interior paint is to wait 1 to 2 hours before the second coat. That is the minimum in normal conditions, around room temperature with moderate humidity. Cool or damp rooms take longer. Oil-based paint takes much longer than latex; check the can.

Painting the second coat too early pulls up the first one and leaves drag marks. If the wall still feels tacky or cool to the touch, wait.

## How coats change how much paint you buy

Every extra coat adds the full wall area again. In a 12 x 12 ft bedroom with 8 ft walls, one coat on the walls takes about 1 gallon, two coats about 2 gallons, and three coats close to 3. The [paint calculator](/blog/paint-calculator/) lets you switch between one, two and three coats and see the difference before you buy.

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need two coats if I use paint and primer in one?

Usually, yes. Paint-and-primer products hide better than plain paint, but they still work best in two coats unless you are repainting a similar color over sound walls.

### Is it OK to do one coat on a ceiling?

If the ceiling is white and you are painting it white again, one coat is often fine. Water stains need a stain-blocking primer first, or they bleed through.

### Can I paint a second coat the next day?

Yes. Waiting overnight is fine and often gives a better result. Just make sure the room stays clean and dust-free in between.

### How many coats does trim need?

Two, as a rule. Trim gets bumped and cleaned more than walls, and glossy paint shows thin spots easily.
